items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: I was in Pharoah’s band at the time.

ctx.x: Yeah. Excellent. So when you got to New York we talked about you felt pretty good about your musicianship and it sounds to me like you had less of a struggle than a lot of other musicians. I don’t know if you can compare your experience to someone else, but you played from ’69 to ’72 if my facts are correct, both with Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders simultaneously? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
Mostly with Pharoah. I was in Pharoah’s band at the time. Occasionally I’d play a concert with Alice.
Can you describe, first, a recording session with Pharoah Sanders. What did you know beforehand, if anything, when you went to the session? Had you played the music live?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: So when you played with Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders did you feel comfortable with the intent, the seeming intent of the music?

ctx.x: Yes I did, and it did have a certain — it’s so interesting how some undefinable magic created by four people is felt by a lot of people. And that it becomes an event.

Yeah. In all honesty that was one of the greatest, most precious moments of my career playing with those guys. They were just — there was a spirit in the group that to this day is relatively unsurpassed this side of Pharoah Sanders who played a lot of spiritual music. But the Charles Lloyd situation was more not only individually collected, you know, spirits that felt something, but there was a quality of intellect that would fashion these things that would come about musically on the stage. And I just heard the…
Yes. I think he’s had a stroke and probably won’t be playing again is what he expressed.
